detail.description: The rewrite routes money through IEEE-754 binary floating point, which cannot represent decimal cents exactly, so `toMinor` now loses or gains a cent on precisely the half-cent inputs that rounding rules exist for. `parseFloat("1.005") * 100` is `100.49999999999999`, so `Math.round` returns **100** — a cent silently vanishes. But `parseFloat("1.115") * 100` is exactly `111.5`, which rounds **up**

The `await` was removed from `credit(bet)`, so `settle()` no longer waits for the credit to complete before executing `await markSettled(bet)`. The function's stated contract — "credits the player, then marks the bet settled" — is now violated in two ways. First, ordering: `markSettled` is invoked while the credit is still in flight, so the bet can be recorded as settled before (or without) the pl

`settle()` has no logging or correlation context. When a settlement fails partway, there is no record of which bet was in flight, which of the two steps completed, or what the underlying error was — an operator paged at 3am has only a stack trace from an unhandled rejection with no bet identifier attached to the settlement attempt.

`settle()` takes `credit` and `markSettled` as injected callbacks but offers no guarantee that either is idempotent, and performs no dedup of its own. Even with the `await` restored, the "credit succeeded, markSettled failed" cell of the outcome table leaves a caller with no safe action: retrying `settle()` double-credits, and not retrying strands a settled-in-fact bet as unsettled in the record.

The new pattern `/^([a-zA-Z0-9]+)+@[^@\s]{1,255}$/` contains a nested quantifier — `+` applied to a group that is itself `[a-zA-Z0-9]+` — over an overlapping character class. This is the textbook catastrophic-backtracking construction. For any input that is a run of alphanumerics followed by a character that is neither alphanumeric nor `@`, the engine must try every partition of that run before it

Restricting the local part to `[a-zA-Z0-9]` rejects a large share of real, deliverable addresses. Verified against both patterns: `a.b@x.com`, `first+tag@x.com`, `a_b@x.com` and `a-b@x.com` all pass the old regex and all fail the new one. Dots are ubiquitous in `firstname.lastname@` corporate addressing, and `+`-tagging is standard on Gmail and most modern providers; `_` and `-` are common as well
